sections.heading: The legal rule
sections.body: 29. The exceptions in sections 25, 26 and 27 do not extend to acts which are offences independently of any harm which they may cause, or be intended to cause, or be known to be likely to cause, to the person giving the consent, or on whose behalf the consent is given

sections.heading: Essential ingredients
sections.body: The exceptions in sections 25, 26 and 27 do not extend to acts which are offences independently of any harm which they may cause, or be intended to cause, or be known to be likely to cause, to the person giving the consent, or on whose behalf the consent is given

sections.heading: Statutory illustrations
sections.body: Causing miscarriage (unless caused in good faith for the purpose of saving the life of the woman) is an offence independently of any harm which it may cause or be intended to cause to the woman. Therefore, it is not an offence “by reason of such harm”; and the consent of the woman or of her guardian to the causing of such miscarriage does not justify the act

learningObjectives: Understand the limits of consent regarding acts that are intrinsically criminal under BNS s. 29.
Examine why consent cannot excuse offences that violate public morals, public order, or independent statutory prohibitions.
Differentiate harm to consenting person from intrinsic statutory offences.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 29 provides that the exceptions in sections 25, 26 and 27 do not extend to acts which are offences independently of any harm which they may cause, or be intended to cause, or be known to be likely to cause, to the person giving the consent, or on whose behalf the consent is given.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Consent can only wipe out the private wrong of bodily harm to the consenting individual; it cannot legalize an act that the law penalizes independently as a public crime or intrinsic statutory offence.
statutoryFramework: Chapter III — General Exceptions, BNS s. 29 (corresponding to IPC s. 91).
Qualifying scope: Acts as a limitation on ss. 25, 26, and 27.
Rule: If the act is an offence 'independently of harm caused' to the person, consent is irrelevant.
Classic statutory application: Unlawful termination of pregnancy / causing miscarriage without medical justification.
essentialIngredients: The act is sought to be defended under s. 25, 26, or 27 on grounds of consent.
The act constitutes an offence in itself, independently of any harm caused to the consenting party.
By operation of s. 29, the consent defence is entirely excluded.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Sections 25, 26, and 27 allow consent to excuse harm inflicted upon a person. Section 29 introduces an essential boundary: you cannot consent to a crime. For example, voluntarily causing miscarriage (unless in good faith to save the mother's life under medical termination laws) is an independent statutory offence against unborn life and public policy. The pregnant woman's consent to the abortion cannot shield the performer under s. 26 because the act is an offence independently of the harm caused to the woman.
examples: Teaching example (Illegal abortion): A pregnant woman freely consents to an unqualified person performing an illegal abortion for non-medical reasons. The procedure causes minor bleeding. The performer cannot plead s. 26 consent because causing miscarriage is an independent offence; s. 29 excludes the exception.

Teaching example (Consent to treason or rioting): A person consents to being struck during an unlawful assembly or armed insurrection. The participation in the riot is an independent crime; consent cannot be pleaded.
distinctions: Private harm vs Independent public crime: Private bodily injury can be consented to within limits; independent public crimes cannot be consented to.
Section 26 vs Section 29: Section 26 protects surgery done for medical benefit; Section 29 bars using consent to justify acts that remain crimes in their own right.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether a person who assisted another in committing an illegal, prohibited act with the other's full consent can invoke s. 25 or 26.
Rule: Section 29 bars the defence of consent if the act is an offence independently of harm to the consenting party.
Application: Check whether the act charged (e.g. unlawful female feticide) is an independent statutory offence. If so, consent is legally immaterial.
Conclusion: The consent defence is barred by s. 29.
